_notes: Chronology: dates follow a ministry from the Baptism c. AD 29 (Luke 3:1, as in data.js) to the Crucifixion in April AD 33, with Passovers in AD 30 (John 2), 31, 32 (John 6) and 33. Robertson himself dated the Crucifixion AD 30 or 29; the order of events is his either way.

Split sections: §33 → §33a judeanbaptism (jesus lane, judeacountry) and §33b johnaenon (john lane, aenon). §34 → §34a leavejudea (jesus) and §34b johnarrested (herod lane, machaerus). All other sections are one event each.
Lanes: only jesus, john and herod are used. No new lanes.

Places: all ids come from places-canon.txt (judeanwild, cana, capernaum, temple [reused], bethabara [reused], judeacountry, aenon, machaerus, jacobswell, galilee). Machaerus is also listed in data.js CONTEXT; if it becomes a PLACE it should be dropped from CONTEXT.
Each journey event has a "route" field ([lon,lat] waypoints); the map builder needs to read it. Events without a journey have no route.

Scripture: Bible Gateway's RSVCE prints pronunciation marks in names (Nathan′a-el, Caper′na-um, Ae′non, Hero′di-as). These were normalized to plain spellings (Nathanael, Capernaum, Aenon, Herodias), as data.js does for names. No other changes were needed: none of these verses contain thee/thou.

Art: for John's Temple cleansing (§31) this batch uses El Greco (WGA10541) and Rembrandt's 1635 etching (NGA 9891). Batch 4a has said it will use Giotto's Scrovegni Expulsion and Tissot's "Jesus Forbids the Carrying of Loads" for §129, so there is no clash.
leavejudea (§34a) has no art: I found no fitting public-domain work for this short transition. art is [], as for some events in data.js.
galileearrival (§36) uses Tissot's pen-and-ink study "Women of Galilee" as a stand-in; there is no well-known artwork of John 4:43–45. The lead may prefer a landscape photo of Lower Galilee.
Samaritan woman: I first downloaded Annibale Carracci's "Christ and the Samaritan Woman" (Google Art Project file) but could not confirm which museum holds that version, so I used Tissot instead.

aenon.name: Aenon near Salim
aenon.note: John 3:23 says John baptized at Aenon ("springs") near Salim "because there was much water there." The site is uncertain. Eusebius (4th century) places it in the Jordan Valley about 8 Roman miles south of Scythopolis (Beth-shean), where many springs rise. Other proposals place it near the village of Salim east of Shechem, or east of the Jordan.

cana.name: Cana
cana.note: Cana of Galilee was Nathanael's home town (John 21:2). Two sites are proposed. Kafr Kanna, about 4 miles northeast of Nazareth, holds the Franciscan Wedding Church and the pilgrim tradition. Khirbet Qana, a ruined hilltop about 8 miles north of Nazareth, is favored by many archaeologists; excavations there found a Jewish village of Jesus' time and a cave venerated by early pilgrims.

capernaum.name: Capernaum
capernaum.note: A fishing town on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee, on the road toward Damascus. It became Jesus' home base in Galilee (Matthew 9:1 calls it "his own city"). The white limestone synagogue of the 4th–5th century stands on the black basalt foundations of an earlier one, and a modern church hovers over the house honored as Peter's.

galilee.name: Towns and villages of Galilee
galilee.note: Lower Galilee, the hill country west of the Sea of Galilee ruled by Herod Antipas. It was dense with farming villages and small towns linked by roads. The point stands for Jesus' movements through the region rather than one place.

jacobswell.name: Jacob's Well, Sychar
jacobswell.note: At the foot of Mount Gerizim, the Samaritans' holy mountain, near ancient Shechem (Tell Balata) in today's Nablus. The well is very deep and has been venerated since at least the 4th century. A Greek Orthodox church, completed in 2007, now stands over it. Sychar is usually placed at the village of Askar nearby.

judeacountry.name: Judean countryside
judeacountry.note: John 3:22 says only that Jesus and his disciples went "into the land of Judea" and stayed there baptizing. No town is named. The point marks the Judean countryside outside Jerusalem, toward the Jordan.

judeanwild.name: Judean Wilderness (Mount of Temptation)
judeanwild.note: The Gospels say only "the wilderness." The barren hills between Jerusalem and the Jordan fit the scene. Since at least the 4th century, Jabal Quruntul, the cliff just west of Jericho, has been honored as the Mount of Temptation; the Greek Orthodox Monastery of the Temptation clings to its face.

machaerus.name: Machaerus
machaerus.note: A Herodian fortress-palace on a hilltop east of the Dead Sea, in today's Jordan. Josephus (Antiquities 18.5.2) names it as the place where Herod Antipas imprisoned and beheaded John the Baptist. Excavations have uncovered the palace courtyard, baths and a ritual bath.

events.title: The temptation in the wilderness
events.summary: Straight after his baptism the Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness. He fasts forty days and is tempted by the devil: to turn stones into bread, to throw himself down from the pinnacle of the Temple, and to worship Satan in return for all the kingdoms of the world. Each time he answers with a word from Deuteronomy. Mark adds that he was with the wild beasts, and angels ministered to him. Where Israel failed in its forty years in the desert, Jesus stays faithful.
events.stay: Forty days alone in the wilderness, fasting.
events.journey: About 8 miles west across the Jordan and past Jericho into the hills, if the traditional Mount of Temptation is the place.

scripture.text: Then Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil.

And the tempter came and said to him, "If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become loaves of bread." But he answered, "It is written, 'Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.'"
Then Jesus said to him, "Begone, Satan! for it is written, 'You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve.'"

echoes.note: Israel's forty years of testing in the wilderness, and the verse Jesus quotes: "man does not live by bread alone."
Moses fasted forty days and forty nights on Sinai.

art.title: The Temptations of Christ
art.description: The three temptations play out in the background: at top left the devil, dressed as a hermit, offers Christ stones; at the center they stand on the roof of the Temple; at top right Christ drives the unmasked devil off a mountain while angels set a table. In the foreground a high priest receives a sacrifice before a crowd.
art.significance: One of the wall frescoes painted for Pope Sixtus IV by the leading painters of the day, decades before Michelangelo's ceiling. It faces Botticelli's scenes from the life of Moses on the opposite wall.
art.symbolism: The Temple is modeled on the façade of the Hospital of Santo Spirito in Rome, rebuilt by Sixtus IV. The foreground sacrifice, often read as a leper's purification, sets the old law beside Christ, the new.
art.impact: Seen by millions of visitors to the Sistine Chapel every year, though most look up at the ceiling and miss it.

art.title: Christ in the Wilderness
art.description: Christ sits alone on a gray boulder in a stony desert at first light, worn and barefoot, his hands clenched together in his lap.
art.significance: A founding work of Russian Realism, shown at the second exhibition of the Peredvizhniki ("Wanderers") in 1872 and bought by Pavel Tretyakov for his gallery.
art.symbolism: There is no devil, angel or halo. The struggle is entirely inward: the knotted hands carry the weight of the choice Christ must make.
art.impact: In his letters Kramskoi described it as the moment of decision every person faces, between serving God and serving oneself. It remains one of the best-known religious paintings in Russia.

events.orderNote: Matthew gives the order bread, pinnacle, mountain; Luke has bread, mountain, pinnacle, perhaps so that the scene ends in Jerusalem, as his Gospel does. Matthew's "then" and "again" suggest he keeps the actual sequence. The second or third temptation takes Jesus to the Temple in Jerusalem, so not all of it happens on the mountain.

Mt.text: Then Jesus said to him, "Begone, Satan! for it is written, 'You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve.'"

Mk.text: And he was in the wilderness forty days, tempted by Satan; and he was with the wild beasts; and the angels ministered to him.

Lk.text: And when the devil had ended every temptation, he departed from him until an opportune time.

events.title: John's testimony to the delegation from Jerusalem
events.summary: The Jewish leaders in Jerusalem send priests and Levites to ask John who he is. He says plainly that he is not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the prophet. He is only the voice crying in the wilderness. He baptizes with water, but one already stands among them whose sandal he is not worthy to untie. Robertson notes that the priests and Levites were Sadducees, sent at the prompting of the Pharisees.
events.stay: John was baptizing at Bethany beyond the Jordan.

scripture.text: And this is the testimony of John, when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him, "Who are you?" He confessed, he did not deny, but confessed, "I am not the Christ."
John answered them, "I baptize with water; but among you stands one whom you do not know, even he who comes after me, the thong of whose sandal I am not worthy to untie."

echoes.note: The promise that Elijah would return before the day of the Lord, behind the question "Are you Elijah?"
Moses' promise of a prophet like himself: "the prophet" they ask about.

art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.title: Saint John the Baptist and the Pharisees
art.description: John, barefoot on a rocky ledge, stretches out his arm toward a crowd of listeners, soldiers and robed men who have come out to the wilderness. Two elders sit apart on the rocks, watching.
art.significance: Part of Tissot's series of some 350 scenes from the life of Christ, painted after research trips to Palestine.
art.symbolism: The rough desert prophet stands above the crowd, while the questioners from Jerusalem keep their distance.
art.impact: Tissot's Life of Christ was a sensation in Paris, London and New York in the 1890s; the Brooklyn Museum bought the whole series in 1900.

events.orderNote: John's Gospel does not narrate the baptism or the temptation. Most harmonies, Robertson's among them, place this delegation at the end of the forty days, since the next day (John 1:29) John sees Jesus coming toward him. John denies being Elijah, while Jesus later says John is the Elijah who was to come (Matthew 11:14): John denies being Elijah in person, Jesus speaks of his role.

events.title: "Behold, the Lamb of God"
events.summary: The day after the delegation, John sees Jesus coming toward him and points him out to the crowd as the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. He explains how he knew him: God had told him that the one on whom he saw the Spirit descend and remain would baptize with the Holy Spirit. John saw it happen at the baptism. Now he bears public witness that Jesus is the Son of God.
events.journey: About 8 miles back from the wilderness to the Jordan.

scripture.text: And John bore witness, "I saw the Spirit descend as a dove from heaven, and it remained on him.

I myself did not know him; but he who sent me to baptize with water said to me, 'He on whom you see the Spirit descend and remain, this is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit.' And I have seen and have borne witness that this is the Son of God."

echoes.note: The servant led "like a lamb that is led to the slaughter." The Passover lamb (Exodus 12) is also in view.
"The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him": the promised shoot from Jesse.

art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.title: Saint John the Baptist Sees Jesus from Afar
art.description: John stands above a rocky riverbed with a crowd sitting below him. He raises his arms toward a small white figure far off on the hillside: Jesus, coming toward him.
art.significance: Tissot illustrates John 1:29 literally: "he saw Jesus coming toward him."
art.symbolism: The distance between the two figures marks the moment of recognition before John speaks.
art.impact: Shows the river country beside the Jordan as Tissot observed it in the 1880s.

events.title: The first disciples
events.summary: John again points out Jesus as the Lamb of God, and two of his own disciples follow Jesus and spend the day with him. One is Andrew, who finds his brother Simon and tells him "We have found the Messiah"; Jesus names Simon Cephas, Peter, "Rock." The next day Jesus finds Philip of Bethsaida, and Philip brings Nathanael, who is won over when Jesus tells him he saw him under the fig tree. The unnamed second disciple is traditionally John, son of Zebedee, the Gospel's author.
events.stay: The two disciples "stayed with him that day," from about the tenth hour.

scripture.text: He first found his brother Simon, and said to him, "We have found the Messiah" (which means Christ). He brought him to Jesus. Jesus looked at him, and said, "So you are Simon the son of John? You shall be called Cephas" (which means Peter).

Philip found Nathanael, and said to him, "We have found him of whom Moses in the law and also the prophets wrote, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph." Nathanael said to him, "Can anything good come out of Nazareth?" Philip said to him, "Come and see."
And he said to him, "Truly, truly, I say to you, you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man."

echoes.note: Jacob's dream of angels ascending and descending on a ladder: Jesus himself is now the meeting place of heaven and earth.

art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.title: The Calling of Saint John and Saint Andrew
art.description: Two young men follow Jesus along the riverbank as he turns to ask, "What do you seek?"
art.significance: Tissot follows John's Gospel, where the first disciples come from John the Baptist's circle at the Jordan, not from the boats in Galilee.
art.symbolism: Jesus turning back to them is the first invitation of the Gospel: "Come and see."
art.impact: One of few well-known images of this quiet scene, often overshadowed by the Synoptic call of the fishermen.

art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.title: Nathaniel Under the Fig Tree
art.description: People rest on carpets in the shade of fig trees on a green slope above the water. Tissot sets Nathanael's fig tree in an everyday Galilean scene.
art.significance: Shows the moment Jesus refers to when he tells Nathanael, "when you were under the fig tree, I saw you."
art.symbolism: Sitting under one's fig tree was a biblical image of peace and of study of the law (Micah 4:4).
art.impact: Jesus' words about the fig tree convince Nathanael that Jesus knows him; Tissot imagines the ordinary place where Nathanael was seen.

events.orderNote: These are the first meetings. The Synoptic call by the lake to leave the nets and follow him (Matthew 4:18–22) comes months later, in Galilee. Robertson notes the four successive days of John 1:19, 29, 35 and 43, and the "third day" of John 2:1, making a full first week.

events.title: The wedding at Cana
events.summary: Jesus, his mother and his new disciples are guests at a wedding in Cana. When the wine runs out, Mary tells Jesus and then tells the servants to do whatever he says. He has them fill six stone jars, used for Jewish purification, with water, and it becomes wine better than what was served first. John calls it the first of his signs: it reveals his glory, and his disciples believe in him.
events.journey: About 75 miles up the Jordan Valley and across into the Galilean hills, a hard walk of about three days.

scripture.text: When the wine failed, the mother of Jesus said to him, "They have no wine." And Jesus said to her, "O woman, what have you to do with me? My hour has not yet come." His mother said to the servants, "Do whatever he tells you."

and said to him, "Every man serves the good wine first; and when men have drunk freely, then the poor wine; but you have kept the good wine until now." This, the first of his signs, Jesus did at Cana in Galilee, and manifested his glory; and his disciples believed in him.

echoes.note: The Lord's feast for all peoples, "of wine on the lees well refined."
Pharaoh tells the Egyptians, "Go to Joseph; what he says to you, do," which Mary's words echo.

art.title: The Marriage at Cana
art.description: The guests sit at a long table against striped hangings, beneath a carved wooden gallery. At right a stout steward drinks the new wine beside a row of great stone jars.
art.significance: Part of the fresco cycle that broke from flat Byzantine style and gave figures weight and real space.
art.symbolism: Christ blesses from the end of the table; Mary's raised hand recalls her words, "Do whatever he tells you."
art.impact: The portly, wine-tasting steward is one of Giotto's best-loved touches of everyday humor.

art.title: The Marriage at Cana
art.description: A calm wedding feast in a Flemish hall with a view of a city square. Christ blesses from the table beside Mary while servants pour from jugs over the stone jars; the donor Jean de Sedano and his wife kneel at the sides.
art.significance: Painted in Bruges for a Spanish merchant, it shows how patrons had themselves painted into the Gospel scene.
art.symbolism: The wine turned from water was read as a sign of the Eucharist; the donors kneel as if at Mass.
art.impact: A leading work of Gerard David, the last great master of the Bruges school.

events.orderNote: Two sites claim Cana: Kafr Kanna, the traditional pilgrim site near Nazareth, and Khirbet Qana, a ruin about 5 miles further north, which many archaeologists prefer.

events.title: A first stay in Capernaum
events.summary: After the wedding Jesus goes down to Capernaum on the Sea of Galilee with his mother, his brothers and his disciples. They stay only a few days before the Passover. Capernaum, the home of Peter and Andrew, will later become Jesus' base in Galilee.
events.stay: "There they stayed for a few days."
events.journey: About 16 miles, going "down" from the hills to the lakeshore, nearly 700 feet below sea level.

scripture.text: After this he went down to Capernaum, with his mother and his brethren and his disciples; and there they stayed for a few days.

art.title: Capernaum on the Sea of Galilee
art.description: A quick sketch of the lake at Capernaum: a low stone wall and a lone palm in the foreground, the pale blue water and the bare hills of the far shore beyond.
art.significance: Painted on the Polish artist's journey to Palestine, before the modern churches were built over the site.
art.symbolism: The empty shore recalls how small and ordinary the town was where Jesus made his home.
art.impact: A rare painted view of Capernaum from the years when the synagogue ruins were first being explored.

art.credit: Photo: Berthold Werner, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
art.title: The synagogue of Capernaum
art.location: Capernaum National Park, Sea of Galilee
art.description: The white limestone walls and columns of the later synagogue rise behind palms, above dark basalt house foundations of the ancient town.
art.significance: The standing synagogue dates from the 4th–5th century AD. Beneath it, excavators found basalt walls of an earlier building, which many identify with the synagogue where Jesus taught (Mark 1:21).
art.symbolism: The white stone set on black basalt is a picture of the town's layers: the later Jewish community built on the place remembered from Jesus' day.
art.impact: Excavated and partly rebuilt by Franciscan archaeologists in the 20th century; it is one of the most visited sites in Galilee.

events.orderNote: "His brethren" are understood in Catholic and Orthodox tradition as relatives (cousins or Joseph's sons), and by many Protestants as later children of Mary and Joseph.

events.title: The first cleansing of the Temple
events.summary: At Passover Jesus goes up to Jerusalem. In the Temple courts he finds men selling oxen, sheep and pigeons, and money-changers at their tables. He makes a whip of cords, drives them out, overturns the tables and says, "You shall not make my Father's house a house of trade." Asked for a sign, he says, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." He spoke of his body, as the disciples understood after the Resurrection.
events.stay: In Jerusalem for the week of the Passover feast.
events.journey: About 100 miles, nearly a week on foot, probably down the Jordan Valley and up through Jericho with the Passover pilgrims.

scripture.text: And making a whip of cords, he drove them all, with the sheep and oxen, out of the temple; and he poured out the coins of the money-changers and overturned their tables. And he told those who sold the pigeons, "Take these things away; you shall not make my Father's house a house of trade."

Jesus answered them, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." The Jews then said, "It has taken forty-six years to build this temple, and will you raise it up in three days?" But he spoke of the temple of his body.

echoes.note: "Zeal for your house has consumed me," which the disciples remembered (John 2:17).
"There shall no longer be a trader in the house of the Lord of hosts on that day."

art.title: The Purification of the Temple
art.description: Christ swings a whip at the center of a crowded portico. Traders recoil on the left, while on the right the apostles watch and discuss.
art.significance: El Greco painted this subject again and again over some forty years; it was one of his most personal themes.
art.symbolism: The reliefs in the background show the expulsion from Eden and the sacrifice of Isaac: sin and its punishment, and the promise of redemption. In Counter-Reformation Spain the scene also stood for the purifying of the Church.
art.impact: Among the most famous images of the cleansing; its twisting, elongated figures show El Greco's mature style.

art.credit: National Gallery of Art, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
art.title: Christ Driving the Money Changers from the Temple
art.location: National Gallery of Art, Washington (this impression)
art.description: Christ raises a whip of cords above his head as money-changers tumble over their tables and a frightened ox bolts.
art.significance: Rembrandt borrowed the figure of Christ from a Dürer woodcut, but filled the scene with his own chaotic energy.
art.symbolism: The whip of cords is the detail found only in John's account (John 2:15).
art.impact: Prints like this spread Rembrandt's Bible scenes across Europe in his lifetime.

events.orderNote: John puts a cleansing at the first Passover; Matthew, Mark and Luke put one in Passion Week. Many scholars think there was one event, which John moved forward for theological reasons; Robertson, with many others, holds there were two, at the start and close of the ministry. Robertson dates this Passover AD 27; the date here follows this map's chronology (crucifixion AD 33).

events.title: Nicodemus comes by night
events.summary: During the feast many believe in Jesus because of his signs, but he does not trust himself to them. Nicodemus, a Pharisee and a member of the ruling council, comes to him by night. Jesus tells him that no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born anew, of water and the Spirit. The talk leads to the most quoted verse of the Gospel, John 3:16. Nicodemus will reappear defending Jesus (John 7:50) and helping to bury him (John 19:39).
events.stay: Jesus was in Jerusalem for the Passover; the meeting place is not named.

scripture.text: Jesus answered him, "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born anew, he cannot see the kingdom of God."
The wind blows where it wills, and you hear the sound of it, but you do not know whence it comes or whither it goes; so it is with every one who is born of the Spirit."
For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.

echoes.note: Moses lifts up the bronze serpent so that those who look on it live; "so must the Son of man be lifted up" (John 3:14).
God's promise to sprinkle clean water and put a new spirit within his people.

art.title: Nicodemus Visiting Jesus
art.location: Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts, Philadelphia
art.description: Jesus and the white-bearded Nicodemus sit facing each other on a flat rooftop under a deep blue night sky, the town and hills behind them. Warm light glows up from the stairway below.
art.significance: Painted after Tanner's trip to Palestine, where he studied houses and rooftops like this one.
art.symbolism: Nicodemus, in shadow, listens; Jesus, facing us, speaks. The night recalls that Nicodemus came "by night," and John 3:19–21: the light has come into the world.
art.impact: It won the Pennsylvania Academy's Lippincott Prize in 1900 and helped make Tanner the best-known African American painter of his day.

art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.title: Interview between Jesus and Nicodemus
art.description: Jesus and Nicodemus sit close together on a mat in a plain room, lit by a small lamp on a stand. Their sandals lie on the floor below.
art.significance: Unlike Tanner, who chose a rooftop, Tissot sets the meeting indoors, as an intimate, whispered talk.
art.symbolism: The night setting reflects John's note that Nicodemus came "by night," perhaps for fear of others.
art.impact: Gives a vivid sense of a quiet, private talk between a teacher of Israel and Jesus.

events.orderNote: Ancient Greek had no quotation marks, so it is unclear where Jesus' words end and John's own reflection begins; many readers think the speech ends at verse 15 and verses 16–21 are the evangelist's comment.

events.title: Jesus' disciples baptize in Judea
events.summary: After the Passover Jesus goes out into the Judean countryside with his disciples. He stays there for some time, and they baptize the people who come; John 4:2 adds that Jesus himself did not baptize, only his disciples. Crowds begin to go to Jesus rather than John. This little-known Judean ministry may have lasted several months.
events.stay: "There he remained with them and baptized": probably several months.
events.journey: A short way out of Jerusalem into the Judean countryside; John names no town.

scripture.text: After this Jesus and his disciples went into the land of Judea; there he remained with them and baptized.

art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.title: The Disciples of Jesus Baptize
art.description: At a pool reached by worn stone steps beneath an arch, men in white mantles guide people down into the water while a crowd watches from the wall above.
art.significance: One of very few artworks of this brief scene from John 3:22 and 4:2.
art.symbolism: The disciples, not Jesus, perform the baptisms, as John 4:2 is careful to note.
art.impact: Brings to light a part of the ministry most readers overlook.

events.title: "He must increase, but I must decrease"
people: A Jew who disputes about purifying
events.summary: John is now baptizing farther north at Aenon near Salim, where there is much water, since he has not yet been put in prison. His disciples complain that everyone is going to Jesus. John answers that he is only the friend of the bridegroom, who rejoices to hear the bridegroom's voice. His joy is now full: Jesus must increase and he must decrease.
events.stay: John baptized at Aenon "because there was much water there."

scripture.text: John also was baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because there was much water there; and people came and were baptized.

He who has the bride is the bridegroom; the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom's voice; therefore this joy of mine is now full. He must increase, but I must decrease."

echoes.note: "As the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you": God as Israel's bridegroom.

art.title: Saint John the Baptist
art.description: A smiling young John emerges from deep darkness, holding a slender reed cross and pointing upward.
art.significance: Believed to be among Leonardo's last paintings; it was still with him in France at the end of his life.
art.symbolism: The raised finger points away from himself toward heaven and the one to come: "He must increase, but I must decrease."
art.impact: Its soft modeling (sfumato) and enigmatic smile have fascinated viewers since the Renaissance.

events.orderNote: Aenon's site is uncertain: the Jordan Valley south of Beth-shean (Eusebius), the springs near Salim east of Shechem in Samaria, or east of the Jordan. Robertson notes John may have been preaching to Samaritans. Readers disagree whether verses 31–36 are still John's words or the evangelist's.

events.title: Jesus leaves Judea
events.summary: The Pharisees hear that Jesus is making and baptizing more disciples than John. When Jesus learns this, and hears that John has been handed over to prison, he leaves Judea and returns to Galilee. Robertson reads both reasons together: the rising hostility of the Pharisees, and the danger shown by John's arrest. The shortest road north runs through Samaria.

scripture.text: Now when the Lord knew that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John (although Jesus himself did not baptize, but only his disciples), he left Judea and departed again to Galilee.
Now when he heard that John had been arrested, he withdrew into Galilee;

echoes.note: "Galilee of the nations... the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light," which Matthew 4:14–16 quotes for Jesus' move to Galilee.

events.orderNote: John's Gospel says only that the Pharisees heard of his success; Matthew and Mark tie the return to Galilee to John's arrest. Mark and Matthew pass straight from the temptation to Galilee, so without John's Gospel we would not know of this earlier Judean ministry.

Mt.text: Now when he heard that John had been arrested, he withdrew into Galilee;

Mk.text: Now after John was arrested, Jesus came into Galilee, preaching the gospel of God,

Lk.text: And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit into Galilee, and a report concerning him went out through all the surrounding country.

Jn.text: he left Judea and departed again to Galilee. He had to pass through Samaria.

events.title: Herod Antipas imprisons John
events.summary: John has rebuked Herod Antipas for taking Herodias, his brother's wife, and for all his other evil deeds. Herod adds this to the rest and shuts John up in prison. Josephus says the prison was the fortress of Machaerus east of the Dead Sea, and gives Herod's political motive: he feared John's influence over the people might lead to a revolt. John will remain there until his execution.
events.stay: John was held in the fortress of Machaerus, by Josephus' account, for many months.

scripture.text: But Herod the tetrarch, who had been reproved by him for Herodias, his brother's wife, and for all the evil things that Herod had done, added this to them all, that he shut up John in prison.

echoes.note: Elijah confronts King Ahab, whose wife Jezebel then seeks his life; Herod and Herodias play the same roles against John, the new Elijah.
The law forbidding a man to marry his brother's wife, the ground of John's rebuke.

art.title: Machaerus
art.description: The cone-shaped hill of Machaerus rises from the dry hills east of the Dead Sea, which shines in the haze behind it. A few re-erected columns of Herod's palace stand on the flat summit.
art.significance: Josephus names Machaerus as the place where Herod Antipas imprisoned and executed John the Baptist.
art.symbolism: A remote desert stronghold, close to the Perean country where John preached, but cut off from the crowds.
art.impact: Excavations by Franciscan and later Hungarian archaeologists uncovered the palace and re-erected some of its columns.

events.orderNote: Matthew 14:3–5 and Mark 6:17–20 tell the arrest only later, as a flashback at John's death; Luke mentions it early, in Luke 3:19–20, to close John's story. Josephus (Antiquities 18.5.2) names Machaerus.

events.title: The Samaritan woman at Jacob's Well
events.summary: Tired from the journey, Jesus sits by Jacob's Well at noon and asks a Samaritan woman for a drink, breaking the custom that Jews and Samaritans had no dealings. He offers her living water, reveals that she has had five husbands, and tells her that true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth. Then he tells her plainly that he is the Messiah. She runs to tell her town, many Samaritans believe, and they call him "the Savior of the world."
events.stay: At the Samaritans' request Jesus stayed two days in Sychar.
events.journey: About 30 to 40 miles north along the ridge road through the hills of Samaria, a two-day walk; he reaches the well about noon.

scripture.text: Jesus said to her, "Every one who drinks of this water will thirst again, but whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will never thirst; the water that I shall give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life."
The woman said to him, "I know that Messiah is coming (he who is called Christ); when he comes, he will show us all things." Jesus said to her, "I who speak to you am he."
They said to the woman, "It is no longer because of your words that we believe, for we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this is indeed the Savior of the world."

echoes.note: Joseph's bones were buried at Shechem, in the plot Jacob bought: the "field that Jacob gave to his son Joseph" (John 4:5).
Jacob meets Rachel at a well, one of several biblical meetings at wells.

art.title: Christ and the Samaritan Woman
art.description: Christ sits on the edge of a six-sided well and speaks with the woman, who balances a red jar on her head. At right the disciples come out of the gate of the walled town of Sychar.
art.significance: A panel from the back of the Maestà, Duccio's great altarpiece for Siena Cathedral, which was later dismantled and scattered among museums.
art.symbolism: The gold background lifts the conversation out of time; the city gate behind recalls that the woman will go back to bring her town to Christ.
art.impact: The Maestà was carried in procession from Duccio's workshop to the cathedral in 1311; its panels are among the treasures of early Italian art.

art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.title: The Woman of Samaria at the Well
art.description: Inside a vaulted stone well-house, Jesus sits wrapped in a white mantle while the woman, in bright striped clothes, lowers a small cup on a rope into the well.
art.significance: Tissot pictures Jacob's Well as he found it in the 1880s, enclosed in the vaulted chamber of a ruined church.
art.symbolism: The woman draws ordinary water while Jesus, seated at rest, speaks of the living water he gives.
art.impact: Brings out the setting John stresses: "the well is deep," and the woman has come alone at midday.

events.orderNote: Robertson notes that Jesus openly says he is the Messiah here (John 4:26), to a Samaritan, while in Judea and Galilee he avoids the title until the end. Jesus' remark that there are "yet four months" to harvest (John 4:35) could date this to about December or January, if it is not a proverb; Robertson thinks it is probably a proverb.

events.title: Jesus arrives in Galilee
events.summary: After two days in Sychar Jesus goes on to Galilee. Though he had said that a prophet has no honor in his own country, the Galileans welcome him. Many had been in Jerusalem at the Passover and seen what he did there. This begins the great Galilean ministry.
events.journey: About 40 to 50 miles north through Samaria and across the Jezreel Valley into Galilee, two or three days on foot.

scripture.text: For Jesus himself testified that a prophet has no honor in his own country. So when he came to Galilee, the Galileans welcomed him, having seen all that he had done in Jerusalem at the feast, for they too had gone to the feast.
